deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page: no formulas, no computations and no derivations. It is a passage of Riemann's natural-philosophical argument about the 'soul of the Earth', which is Fechner-inspired. The argument runs continuously from p. 28 to p. 30.

Context. On p. 28 Riemann argues that the ponderable masses inside, or just beneath, the solidified crust of the Earth are the bearers of the Earth's mental life (Seelenleben). He then asks what the external conditions for a life-process are. He says the empirical regularities of observable life-processes must be the basis, but conclusions transfer to other domains only insofar as those regularities can be explained.

This page lists the 'general experiences about the external conditions of the life-process in the domain of phenomena accessible to us':

(1) The higher, more complete and 'more intense' a life-process is, the more its bearers need protection against external moving causes. These are causes that tend to change the relative position of the parts.

(2) The known physical processes (metabolism, Stoffwechsel) that serve this process as means:
- (a) absorption of gases ('elastic fluids') by liquids;
- (b) endosmosis;
- (c) formation and decomposition of chemical compounds;
- (d) galvanic currents.

(3) The materials of organisms have no recognizable crystalline structure. They are partly solid (very little brittle?), partly gelatinous, partly liquid or gaseous. They are always porous, i.e. noticeably permeable to gases.

(4) Of all chemical elements only the four so-called organic ones (C, H, O, N) are general bearers of the life-process. Among their compounds, specific ones are the 'organizing' constituents of organisms (protein substances, cellulose, etc.).

(5) Organic compounds exist only up to a certain upper temperature limit. They can bear the life-process only down to a certain lower limit.

Commentary 'ad 1'. Changes in the relative position of parts are produced to successively smaller degrees by:
- mechanical forces;
- temperature changes;
- light rays.

The facts behind statement (1) are ordered accordingly:
- (i) Lower organisms can propagate by division, while reproductive (regenerative) capacity gradually decreases in higher animals. This corresponds to sensitivity to mechanical disturbance.
- (ii) Parts of plants are the more sensitive to temperature changes the more intense and highly developed their life-process. Higher animals maintain an almost constant temperature, most perfectly in their most important parts. This corresponds to thermal disturbance.
- (iii) On the next page: the parts of the nervous system serving independent thought are maximally shielded from all these influences.

Where the argument goes (p. 30):
- Statement (1) is explained as follows: the relative position of parts can be determined by internal processes the less it is determined by external ones.
- The Earth's interior realizes such shielding far better than any organic arrangement could.
- Statements (4) and (5) seem to contradict the hypothesis that the hot interior bears the Earth's mental life. Riemann argues they hold only relatively, for our domain of experience.

Logical structure: an inductive list of empirical conditions, followed by a qualitative ordering principle (strength of external disturbance) used to rank the facts. Nothing is computed.
errors: No mathematical errors are possible; the content is qualitative.

The empirical claims reflect 1850s physiology and chemistry. The 'four organic elements' as the sole general bearers of life omits P, S and other essential elements, though the restriction to C, H, O, N was a standard formulation of the time.
The overall argument, that life or thought resides in the Earth's interior, is speculative Naturphilosophie in the tradition of Fechner. It is not a scientific result.

results.what: List of empirical external conditions for life-processes: shielding from external disturbance, metabolic physical processes, non-crystalline porous materials, the four organic elements, a temperature window. Facts are ordered by the decreasing strength of mechanical, thermal and light disturbances.
results.modern_name: None (19th-century Naturphilosophie, 'Erdseele' speculation in the style of Fechner's Zend-Avesta)
results.usually_credited_to: G. T. Fechner (Zend-Avesta, 1851) for the Earth-soul idea; the physiological facts are common knowledge of the period

deep.surprise_reason: The page contains no mathematics. Riemann's interest in Fechner and his Naturphilosophie fragments are well known; parts appear in the Gesammelte Werke under 'Fragmente philosophischen Inhalts'. A pencil note on the previous page ('Von hier an bis S. 32 wohl wegzulassen') suggests the editors deliberately omitted this Earth-soul section. So it is a minor unpublished philosophical detail, of interest to historians of Riemann's worldview but carrying no mathematical novelty.
transcription_corrections: Item 2: the image appears to read 'welche dem Denkprocesse als Mittel dienen' rather than 'dem Lebensprocesse'. The word after 'dem' starts with 'D', which fits the Denkprocess theme of p. 28; this needs verification against the original.
'Proteinstoffe, Cellulose cc' is probably an abbreviation for 'etc.' (u.s.w.).
'in Stufenweise geringerem Grade' should be read as 'in stufenweise geringerem Grade' (lowercase adverb).
'deren allgemeiner Ausdruck unser (?) Satz ist': the editorial (?) is in the manuscript as '(?)'; the reading 'unser' is plausible.
'theils fest (sehr wenig spröde?)': the reading 'spröde' is uncertain in the image but plausible.
